initial_requirements: NJIT needs a secure distance-learning environment that helps professors communicate and work with students online. Virtual-EDU should provide a classroom-like portal where enrolled users can communicate individually or in groups, share and collaborate on learning materials, and participate in online course activities. Administrators will also need to manage the learning environment and its enrolled users.

messages.content: What are the primary success goals for Virtual-EDU from NJIT’s perspective—for example, what outcomes should the platform enable for professors, students, and administrators?

From NJIT’s perspective, the main goal is to make online learning feel organized, secure, and easy to use for everyone involved. Professors should be able to teach, communicate, share materials, and manage class activities without relying on scattered tools, and students should be able to participate, collaborate, and access course content reliably from anywhere. For administrators, the platform should make it straightforward to manage users, courses, and the overall environment while keeping the system secure and under control.

What authentication and access-control requirements should Virtual-EDU enforce for professors, students, and administrators—for example, how users log in, how roles and permissions are assigned, and what actions each role should or should not be allowed to perform?

It should require individual user accounts, and I’d expect login to be tied to NJIT credentials or some other centrally managed authentication rather than shared accounts. Roles would need to be assigned by administration, with professors, students, and admins each seeing only what they’re supposed to see based on course enrollment and job function. Professors should manage their own classes and materials, students should only access the courses they’re enrolled in and participate there, and administrators should have broader management access but still with auditability and restrictions where appropriate.
What are the key business rules and course lifecycle requirements for Virtual-EDU—for example, how courses are created, approved, opened, closed, archived, and who is allowed to perform each action?

I’d expect courses to be created and maintained by administrators, or at least provisioned by them even if professors help set up the content. There should be a clear lifecycle so a course can be opened for enrollment and activity at the start of a term, then closed when the term ends, and archived afterward so records and materials remain available as needed but the course is no longer actively used. I’m not sure yet whether professors should be allowed to request changes or create course shells directly, so that would need to be confirmed with NJIT’s policy.

What communication channels should Virtual-EDU support for professors, students, and administrators—such as announcements, direct messaging, group chat, discussion forums, email notifications, or live video/audio sessions—and are there any requirements for when each channel should be used?

At minimum, I’d expect announcements for class-wide messages, direct messaging for one-on-one communication, and group communication for team work or class discussions. Email notifications should probably be used for important alerts like new announcements, assignment deadlines, or messages when users are not actively in the system. Live video or audio sessions would be important for lectures or office hours, but I’d need to confirm whether Virtual-EDU is supposed to host those natively or just integrate with an existing tool.

For live video or audio sessions such as lectures and office hours, should Virtual-EDU provide the conferencing capability natively within the platform, or should it integrate with an existing external tool—and if integration is preferred, which tool(s) and what level of integration are expected?

My assumption would be that integration is preferred unless NJIT specifically wants to replace an existing conferencing solution, because that’s usually faster and less disruptive for faculty and students. I don’t know which tool NJIT would want to standardize on, so that would need to be confirmed, but the level of integration should at least let users launch a session from the course page and see the meeting link or schedule in context. If we do use an external tool, it should feel embedded enough that professors can schedule sessions and students can join without a lot of extra steps.

Should Virtual-EDU include discussion forums and assignment/deadline management, and if so, what specific behaviors and rules should each support—for example, forum structure and moderation, assignment creation and submission, deadline handling, late work, and any grading or notification expectations?

Yes, I would expect both discussion forums and assignment management to be part of the platform. Forums should probably be organized by course and topic, with professors able to moderate or remove inappropriate content, and students able to post and reply within their enrolled courses. Assignments should let professors post work with deadlines, students submit files or text responses, and the system should handle due dates, late submissions, and notify users about upcoming deadlines or newly posted work.

Should Virtual-EDU include a gradebook and assessment tracking, and if so, what should it record and how should grades be calculated and displayed—for example, who can enter or edit grades, whether students can see grades immediately or only after release, and whether the system should support weighted categories, drops, curves, or other calculation rules?

Yes, I’d expect a gradebook to be included, because that’s a core part of a course portal. Professors should be able to enter and edit grades for their own courses, while students should only be able to view their own results, and whether grades appear immediately or only after release may need to be configurable by the professor. For the calculation rules, I know weighted categories are important, but I’m not sure yet whether NJIT wants drops, curves, or other special grading logic built in, so that would need to be verified.

For grading and assignment deadlines in Virtual-EDU, are there any special rules NJIT wants beyond weighted categories—for example grade drops, curves, extra credit, late-submission grace periods, or other deadline exceptions—and if so, how should those rules work?

I’m not aware of any NJIT-wide special grading rules beyond the basic weighted categories, and I wouldn’t want to assume drops or curves are standard. Extra credit and late work grace periods seem like the kinds of things professors might want to control per course or per assignment, but that would need confirmation. If those are supported, they should probably be configurable by the instructor rather than hard-coded into the system.

For live video/audio sessions and other real-time activities in Virtual-EDU, what scale and performance expectations should the system meet—for example, how many concurrent users or sessions per course, what response or latency targets are acceptable, and are there peak-load periods or other capacity constraints NJIT wants the platform to handle?

I don’t have exact numbers for concurrent users or session capacity, so those limits would need to be confirmed with NJIT and whatever conferencing tool we use. My expectation is that the system should support normal class sizes without noticeable delay and remain usable during peak times like the start of term, exam periods, and scheduled lecture hours. For live sessions, low latency and stable joining should be treated as important, but the precise performance targets aren’t something I can give you yet.

What grading options should instructors be able to configure per course or assignment in Virtual-EDU—for example extra credit, late-work grace periods, drops, curves, or other special grading rules—and how should each option work?

Instructors should at least be able to configure extra credit and some kind of late-work handling per assignment or course, because those are common teaching needs. I would also expect them to control whether an assignment can be dropped from the final grade, but I’m not sure about automatic curves, since that may be more of a departmental policy than a system feature. The exact behavior for each option should probably be course-specific and left to the instructor unless NJIT wants a standard policy enforced across the platform.

Should Virtual-EDU be designed with any specific priorities for mobile use and accessibility—for example, must it work well on phones and tablets, support offline or low-connectivity access, or meet any accessibility standards such as WCAG or NJIT compliance requirements?

Yes, I’d consider mobile support important, because students and professors will likely use phones or tablets at least some of the time. I’m not sure about offline access, and I wouldn’t assume that unless NJIT specifically asks for it, but the platform should handle low-connectivity situations as gracefully as possible. Accessibility should absolutely be a priority, and I’d expect us to align with WCAG and any NJIT accessibility requirements once those are confirmed.

For course materials and student submissions in Virtual-EDU, what should the system retain and for how long—for example, should it keep version history for edited files, and are there specific file types, size limits, virus/malware checks, or other submission restrictions that need to be enforced?

I’d expect the system to retain course materials and submitted assignments for at least the duration of the course, and probably longer if NJIT wants records kept for audit or academic reference. Version history would be useful for edited files, especially for collaborative documents or revised submissions, but I’m not sure whether that has to be kept indefinitely. File type limits, size limits, and malware scanning should definitely be enforced, though the exact allowed formats and thresholds would need to be set by NJIT or the course instructor.

For assignment submissions in Virtual-EDU, which file types should be allowed or blocked, what size limits should apply, and how should malware/security scanning be handled—for example, should the rules be standardized by NJIT, configurable by instructors per course, or both?

I’d lean toward a standard NJIT baseline for allowed file types, size limits, and malware scanning, with instructors able to tighten restrictions if needed for a specific course. I’d expect common academic formats like PDF, Word, PowerPoint, spreadsheets, images, and maybe source-code files for programming courses to be allowed, while executables and obviously risky file types should be blocked. Malware scanning should happen automatically on upload before the file is made available to others, but the exact size caps are something NJIT would have to define.
